There is an overlooked kind of grief that belongs entirely to inanimate things: the loss of resistance. 

For most of human history, the world pushed back. To open a door required the turn of a brass knob that had its own temperamental spring, heavy and cold in winter, carrying the faint metallic tang of a thousand prior palms. To hear music, you had to physically drop a diamond onto a rotating canyon of vinyl, steadying your breath so the stylus wouldn't skate across the grooves. Words required the strike of a key against an inked ribbon, an act of micro-violence that left a physical dent in the pulp of the paper. Even waiting was an architecture of friction—the rotary dial crawling back clockwise with a soft, ratcheting sigh, demanding three seconds of patience between each digit of a lover’s phone number.

Now, we live on ice. 

Everything is a pane of seamless, tempered glass. You swipe, and the universe slides underneath your finger with zero kinetic drag. There are no edges, no latches, no clicks that settle into the bone. The modern interface is designed to make the world feel as though it has no mass at all. You can summon a feast, a car, an argument, or an encyclopedia with the exact same weightless tap. The gesture required to read an obituary is identical to the one required to delete a spam email.

It is miraculous, of course. To complain about it feels like a hollow indulgence, the kind of sentimental nostalgia that forgets how often ribbons snagged, how easily vinyl warped, how agonizingly slow that rotary dial felt when you needed to call an ambulance.

And yet, our minds were built for friction. 

Thought itself is not a frictionless process. It stumbles. It snags on doubt; it catches on the rough edges of contradiction. When we eliminate all resistance from the physical world, we fool ourselves into believing that our inner lives should run with the same terrifying fluency. We expect grief to resolve in three swipes. We expect nuance to fit into a notification. When a relationship requires the slow, grinding effort of an ungreased hinge, we recoil, assuming it must be broken simply because it does not glide.

Lately, I find myself drawn to things that refuse to hurry. 

A cast-iron skillet that takes ten minutes to heat and an hour to scrub and season. A fountain pen that bleeds through cheap paper and demands that you look at the ink drying before you turn the page. The old radio in the garage that doesn’t have presets, only a weighted dial that moves a red needle across a glowing band of frequencies, through static and whistle and foreign tongues, until a song lands with the sudden, fragile luck of a bird touching down on a wire.

These things do not serve us; they negotiate with us. They remind us that we exist in space, bounded by material facts, subject to decay, tethered to gravity. 

There is an immense relief in that negotiation. On the smooth glass screen, you are everywhere and nowhere, an disembodied appetite flicking through an endless corridor of mirrors. But when you take an old, heavy key and turn it until the tumblers fall—heavy, stubborn, and real—the world suddenly has weight again. You are precisely where you stand. The door is locked, or it is open. And for a moment, the silence that follows has a shape you can lean your shoulder against.
